ARUVI — CLOSING SYNTHESIS RE-AUTHORING · SCIENCE · MIDDLE STAGE

You are re-writing ONE unit: the closing whole-chapter synthesis of a chapter's fullest
lesson plan. This unit is served in two situations, and it must be excellent in both:

1. As the FINAL unit of the fullest plan — the class finishes the chapter with it.
2. As ONE EXTRA 40-minute period appended to a SHORTER complete plan of the same
   chapter, whose own final unit (given below) already consolidated the chapter
   yesterday.

THE UNIT YOU ARE WRITING closes the chapter through one fresh, concrete application: a
scenario, artefact, dataset, place or design problem the chapter itself never uses. The
class brings the chapter's concepts; the unit puts them to work in the new setting, and
what the task shows IS the synthesis — the chapter drawn together by using it whole, not
by summarising it.

PROPERTIES OF THE UNIT:
- It opens directly onto its fresh setting: the first band presents the new material and
  puts the first question to the class.
- Every concept or skill it calls on appears in EVERY unit-title map given below — the
  shorter plans differ in what they cover; write only to what all of them share.
- The SHORTEST plan's map is the binding one: applied topics and late enrichment are cut
  from it first, so each concrete demand in your task (a condition to cite, a feature to
  identify, a mechanism to explain) is checked against that map before it is used.
- Every mechanism, apparatus, circuit form or process your setting relies on is one the
  chapter itself teaches — the setting is new, its physics is entirely the chapter's.
- Its vehicle (the kind of task: scenario cards, argument construction, data table,
  concept map, design brief, error correction, narrative trace…) is different in kind
  from every FINAL UNIT given below, and it uses none of the specific stories, quotes,
  objects, questions or catchphrases those final units use.
- Its closing band consolidates what THE TASK ITSELF showed, naming the chapter's central
  ideas as the reason the task worked — earned closure, not ceremony.
- All materials are in its own `materials` list: things any classroom has or the unit
  itself makes.
- Band narration never states a quantity of minutes or any calendar time — the band's
  `minutes` field carries the clock.

  }
}

CHAPTER SUMMARY:

Chapter 4: Exploring Magnets

The chapter opens with a narrative about Reshma, a student from coastal Kerala, who is writing a story about ancient sailors navigating by stars. When clouds obscure the stars in her story, her research leads her to discover the magnetic compass — a device used by travellers for centuries to find directions. This curiosity about compasses and magnets drives the chapter's inquiry. The chapter introduces the history of magnets: naturally occurring lodestones were the first magnets known in ancient times, followed by iron-based artificial magnets. Today, magnets are made from various materials and come in several shapes, including bar magnets, U-shaped magnets, and ring magnets.

4.1 Magnetic and Non-magnetic Materials

This section introduces the fundamental distinction between materials that are attracted to a magnet and those that are not. Students carry out Activity 4.1 ("Let us explore") in which they collect everyday objects, predict whether each will be attracted to a magnet, then test their predictions by bringing a magnet close to each object and recording the outcome in a table. Through this hands-on exploration, students discover that not all materials respond to a magnet. The section establishes the key terms: materials attracted towards a magnet are called magnetic materials (iron, nickel, cobalt, and some of their alloys are examples), while materials that are not attracted are called non-magnetic materials (wood, rubber, plastic, glass, etc.). The activity contains a student-executed investigation component.

4.2 Poles of Magnet

This section focuses on the unequal distribution of magnetic force along a magnet. Activity 4.2 ("Let us investigate") directs students to spread iron filings on a sheet of paper, place a bar magnet over them, and tap the paper to observe where the filings cluster. Students discover that the filings gather most densely near the two ends of the magnet, establishing that magnetic attraction is strongest at these ends. The chapter names these ends the two poles of the magnet — the North pole and the South pole — and notes that this concentration of filings at the poles is true for magnets of any shape, not just bar magnets. Crucially, the section establishes that poles always exist in pairs: a magnet cannot be broken to produce a single pole — every fragment, however small, always has both a North and a South pole. This activity is student-executed.

4.3 Finding Directions

This section develops the directional property of magnets. Activity 4.3 ("Let us experiment") asks students to suspend a bar magnet freely by a thread, allow it to come to rest, mark the line along which it rests, then disturb and repeat. Students find that the magnet always comes to rest along the same north–south line. The section explains that the end pointing north is the North-seeking pole (North pole) and the end pointing south is the South-seeking pole (South pole). Earth's own magnet-like nature is offered as the reason for this consistent alignment. A comparison with a non-magnetised iron bar (which rests in any direction) teaches students how to distinguish a magnet from an unmagnetised piece of metal. The section then explains the structure and use of a magnetic compass: a freely rotating magnetised needle mounted in a circular box with a directional dial, whose North-pointing end is typically painted red. Activity 4.4 ("Let us construct") guides students to magnetise an iron sewing needle by stroking it with a magnet, mount it through a cork floating on water, and use this homemade compass to confirm the north–south alignment. A "Do you know?" sidebar mentions the Indian historical device matsya-yantra, a fish-shaped magnetised iron piece used for sea navigation. Activities 4.3 and 4.4 are both student-executed.

4.4 Attraction and Repulsion between Magnets

This section explores how two magnets interact when brought close to each other. Activity 4.5 ("Let us experiment") uses two labelled bar magnets, one resting on pencils to roll freely, to test what happens when like and unlike poles are brought near each other. Students observe that unlike poles (North and South) attract each other, causing the resting magnet to move towards the approaching pole, while like poles (North–North or South–South) repel each other, causing the magnet to move away. Replacing one magnet with an iron bar reveals that both poles of the iron bar are attracted to both poles of the magnet — establishing repulsion as the definitive test for identifying a magnet. Activity 4.6 ("Let us experiment") uses a magnetic compass and a bar magnet: students bring the North pole of the bar magnet near the compass needle's North pole and observe repulsion (needle moves away), then bring the South pole near the North pole and observe attraction (needle moves closer). Activity 4.7 ("Let us investigate") probes whether non-magnetic materials — wood, cardboard, plastic, glass — block or diminish the magnetic effect on the compass needle. Students find no appreciable change in the needle's deflection when these materials are interposed, leading to the conclusion that magnetic effects can act through non-magnetic materials. Activities 4.5, 4.6, and 4.7 are all student-executed.

4.5 Fun with Magnets

The final section presents three playful applications that reinforce the chapter's concepts through informal experimentation: constructing a magnetic garland by hanging iron filings or pins from a magnet; guiding steel balls through a cardboard maze using a magnet held beneath; and extracting a steel paperclip from water using a magnet without wetting the fingers. A matchbox-car activity using two cars with like poles facing demonstrates repulsion in a dynamic context. A "More to know!" sidebar covers proper magnet storage — keeping pairs with unlike poles adjacent, separated by a wooden piece, with soft-iron keeper bars across the ends — and cautions against heating, dropping, hammering, or placing magnets near electronic devices. The final page illustrates various magnet shapes (bar, disc, cylindrical, ring, spherical) to show that poles always occur in pairs regardless of shape.


======================================================================

CHAPTER SUMMARY:

Chapter 12: Beyond Earth

The chapter opens with a narrative of two children in Nubra, Ladakh, who observe the night sky and experience a sense of wonder about stars, setting the context for exploring objects beyond Earth.

12.1 Stars and Constellations

Stars shine with their own light; some are bright and others dim. Groups of stars that appear to form recognisable patterns are called constellations — a term that in modern usage refers to defined regions of the sky rather than just the star patterns themselves. These patterns were historically used for navigation by sailors and travellers before modern technology. The International Astronomical Union (IAU) officially listed 88 constellations in the early twentieth century, dividing the entire sky into 88 regions. Notable constellations include Orion (depicted as a hunter with a three-star belt), Canis Major (which contains Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky), and Taurus. In Indian astronomy, the term nakshatra denotes specific stars or star groups — Betelgeuse in Orion is known as Ardra, the Pleiades cluster in Taurus as Krittika, and Aldebaran in Taurus as Rohini. Two widely known star patterns are the Big Dipper (in constellation Ursa Major, known in India as Saptarishi) and the Little Dipper (in Ursa Minor), which includes the Pole Star (Polaris, or Dhruva tara). The Pole Star appears nearly stationary in the North direction and is used to locate north in the Northern hemisphere. There is a student activity (Activity 12.1) in which students draw imaginary lines between stars to form their own patterns and invent stories about them.

12.2 Night Sky Watching

The visibility of stars depends on light pollution, smoke, dust, and obstructions such as tall buildings and trees; the night sky is best observed from open, dark locations away from city lights. Light pollution — excessive artificial light at night — reduces the number of stars visible and is a growing global concern; dark sky reserves and parks have been established to preserve dark skies for research. Not all stars and constellations are visible from all locations or at all times of the year; the Pole Star, for example, is not visible from the Southern Hemisphere. Sky mapping apps such as Sky Map and Stellarium help identify stars, constellations, and planets from any given location. The section provides practical preparation guidance for night sky watching: choosing a clear moonless night, waiting about half an hour for eyes to adjust to the dark, and using a compass and printed constellation images. Activities 12.2 and 12.3 are student activities in which learners attempt to locate the Big Dipper, the Pole Star, and the constellation Orion with the star Sirius in the actual night sky.

12.3 Our Solar System

The Sun

The Sun is the star closest to Earth — an extremely hot, spherical ball of gases that produces heat and light, making it the primary source of energy on Earth. Its distance from Earth is about 150 million km, defined as one astronomical unit (au), the standard unit for distances within the solar system. The Sun is about 100 times larger than Earth in diameter; it appears large due to its relative proximity, while far more distant stars appear only as points of light. The Sun regulates climate, seasons, weather, the water cycle, and winds, and is essential for plant growth and all life on Earth.

Planets

A planet is a large, nearly spherical object that revolves around the Sun; this movement is called revolution. The eight planets in order of increasing distance from the Sun are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. The inner four planets are smaller and have solid rocky surfaces; the outer four are much larger, mostly made of gas and ice, and have ring-like structures of dust and rocky material around them. The presence of an atmosphere affects a planet's temperature — Venus is hotter than Mercury despite being farther from the Sun because its thick atmosphere traps heat. Venus is known as the Morning Star or Evening Star; Mars is the Red Planet due to its reddish soil; Earth appears blue from space and is called the Blue Planet. Objects reclassified as dwarf planets — including Pluto — were redefined by the IAU in 2006 when similar small objects were discovered beyond Neptune. Activity 12.4 guides students to locate Venus at dawn (eastern horizon before sunrise) or dusk (western horizon after sunset).

Natural Satellites

Objects that move around planets are commonly called satellites; moons are the natural satellites of planets. Earth has one Moon, Mars has two moons, and Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune have large numbers of moons.

The Moon

Earth's natural satellite, the Moon, is about 3,84,000 km away and takes approximately 27 days to complete one revolution around the Earth. The Moon is about a quarter the size of Earth in diameter and has virtually no atmosphere. Its surface features circular bowl-like structures called craters, formed by the impact of asteroids and rocks from space; without atmosphere, water, or life, these features persist for very long periods. India launched Chandrayaan-1 (2008), Chandrayaan-2 (2019), and Chandrayaan-3 (July 2023); the Vikram lander of Chandrayaan-3 successfully soft-landed near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023, making India the first country to achieve this, and 23 August is now celebrated as National Space Day.

Asteroids

Asteroids are small, rocky, irregularly shaped objects that revolve around the Sun; many orbit in the region between Mars and Jupiter called the asteroid belt. Their sizes range from about 10 m to approximately 500 km.

Comets

Comets are objects from the outer Solar System composed of dust, gases, rocks, and ice; as they approach the Sun, frozen material evaporates to form a visible tail, but they appear dim as they move away. Many comets orbit the Sun periodically — Halley's Comet, for example, appears every 76 years and was last seen in 1986. The Solar System as a whole consists of the Sun, eight planets, their moons, and many smaller objects including asteroids and comets; all objects other than the Sun shine by reflecting sunlight.

12.4 The Milky Way Galaxy

The Milky Way Galaxy (Akasha Ganga) is visible from very dark locations as a faint extended band of light stretching across the night sky. A galaxy contains millions to billions of stars; our entire Solar System is a small part of the Milky Way Galaxy.

12.5 The Universe

Beyond the Milky Way, there are many other galaxies in outer space that scientists study to understand stars, galaxies, and the Universe as a whole. The search for life elsewhere in the Universe is ongoing and directed mainly toward exoplanets — planets discovered orbiting stars other than our Sun — but no evidence of life has been found yet.


======================================================================
